newsitem.title: USA: U.S. buys land marred by Valdez oil spill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. buys land marred by Valdez oil spill.

text.p: The Clinton administration Wednesday bought nearly 60,000 acres of remote Alaska lands marred by the Exxon Valdez oil spill in an effort both to preserve the area and help its inhabitants.

The land was purchased for $34 million from the Chenega Corp, an Alaskan native village, using monies from a $1 billion settlement fund which was set up after the tanker ran aground on Bligh Reef almost eight years ago, spewing 11 million gallons of oil in the nation's worst spill.
A portion of the land will be folded into the Chugach National Forest and the rest will be made into a state park, opening up the land to camping, hiking and other recreation for the first time.

At the same time, injured species such as sockeye salmon, harbour seals and marbled murrelets will be given protection to recuperate and thrive and residents will get a financial boost through expected tourism, federal and state officials said at a signing ceremony for the land deal.

"We can't take back the man-made tragedy of March 24, 1989, but this administration can and will do all that is humanely possible to erase its mark from Alaska's pristine coastline and restore the wildlife, native cultures and local economies that rely on it," said Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman.
"We believe this agreement will help protect and preserve our native culture and the rural Alaskan way of life," said Chuck Totemoff of the Chenega Native Corp.
Totemoff said it had been a tough decision to sell the land but his village had feared that otherwise they would eventually have to harvest timber to earn a living.
"With this agreement our lands will be conserved forever," he said.
The Clinton administration eventually hopes to purchase nearly 760,000 acres in the spill area, including at least 1,000 acres of shoreline and several hundred miles of riverbank.

Chenega became known as "ground-zero" of the spill, Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles said at the signing ceremony. Oil on the beaches was more than a foot thick in many areas and wildlife that was oiled became re-oiled with each succeeding tide.
"Through the dark cloud of spilled oil, there is a silver lining," he said, referring to the agreement.
